title: Nehemiah Hears of Jerusalem and Prays
summary: In the Persian royal city of Susa, Nehemiah, the king's cupbearer, learns from his brother Hanani that the Jews in Judah are in great trouble and that Jerusalem's wall is broken down and its gates burned. He weeps, mourns, fasts, and prays for days. His prayer praises God's covenant faithfulness, confesses the sins of Israel including his own family's, appeals to God's promise through Moses to gather a repentant people, and asks for success when he goes before the king.
story: The book of Ezra ended with the returned community in Jerusalem, its temple rebuilt and its covenant renewed in painful reform. Nehemiah picks up the story about thirteen years after Ezra's arrival (on the traditional dating), and nearly a century after the first return under Cyrus. The temple stands, but the city around it is still defenseless and largely empty. An earlier attempt to rebuild the walls had been stopped by royal order (Ezra 4:7-23), and the news Nehemiah receives may reflect that setback. The chapter introduces a new kind of leader. Zerubbabel was a son of David and Ezra a priest and scholar; Nehemiah is a layman and a court official. His story begins not with action but with grief and prayer, and chapter 2 will show that prayer turning into a bold request.
historical:
The twentieth year is the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes I (2:1), and the month of Chislev (November to December) of that year falls in late 446 BC. Chapter 2 dates Nehemiah's audience with the king to Nisan of the same twentieth year, which in the usual reckoning (with the year beginning in the spring month of Nisan) would come before Chislev. Scholars explain this in different ways: Nehemiah may have counted the king's years from the anniversary of his accession or from an autumn new year, or the text of 1:1 may originally have read the nineteenth year. The difference does not affect the story.

Susa, in southwestern Iran, was one of the royal capitals of the Persian empire, where the kings often spent the winter, and archaeologists have excavated the great palace built there by Darius I. The citadel (Hebrew birah) was the fortified royal quarter. The book of Esther is set in the same city. Hanani, called one of my brothers, may be Nehemiah's full brother; in 7:2 Nehemiah calls him my brother and later puts him in charge of Jerusalem. The broken wall and burned gates Hanani describes could be the lasting damage from the Babylonian destruction of 587 or 586 BC, or more recent damage after the forced stop of Ezra 4:23; many scholars favor the latter because the news came as a fresh shock.
cultural:
A cupbearer in a royal court served the king his wine and often tasted it first to guard against poison. Because the post required absolute trust and gave daily access to the king, cupbearers could become influential advisers. Nehemiah's note at the end of the chapter, that he was the king's cupbearer, explains why his prayer asks for mercy in the sight of this man: he was one of the few people in the empire who could speak to the king directly.

Nehemiah's response follows the patterns of Israelite mourning and prayer: sitting down, weeping, fasting for days, and praying before the God of heaven, a title common in the Persian period. For a Jew in exile, the ruin of Jerusalem was not simply bad news from a distant province. It was the city God had chosen for his name, where Nehemiah's ancestors were buried (2:3), and its disgrace reflected on the honor of Israel's God before the nations. A city without walls in the ancient world was exposed to raids and could not be a secure home, a center of trade, or a place of honor.
literary: The chapter is the opening of the Nehemiah Memoir, written in the first person, which continues through 7:5. After a brief frame (verses 1-4), most of the chapter is a single prayer (verses 5-11). The prayer is built from Scripture. Its opening praise of the great and awesome God who keeps covenant and loving devotion echoes Deuteronomy 7:9 and matches the opening of Daniel's prayer (Daniel 9:4). Its confession uses the language of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28. Its appeal, in verses 8 and 9, combines Leviticus 26:33 (scattering among the nations) with Deuteronomy 30:1-4 (gathering from the farthest horizon) and Deuteronomy 12:5 (the place chosen as a dwelling for God's name). The prayer moves from praise to confession to God's promise to specific petition. The final verse turns suddenly from the God of heaven to this man, and the reader only then learns who Nehemiah is.

outline.t: Praise to the covenant-keeping God and confession of sin
An appeal to God's promise through Moses
A petition for favor before the king

doctrines.note: Nehemiah's prayer is shaped by Scripture: it praises God's character, confesses sin, pleads God's own promises back to him, and then asks for something specific. It shows prayer as sustained (day and night for days) and as preparation for action.

Nehemiah appeals to God as the one who keeps his covenant of loving devotion, and he reminds God of his word to Moses. The covenant included both the warning of scattering and the promise of gathering, and Nehemiah stakes his hope on the second.
Nehemiah includes himself and his father's house in the confession. The promise he claims is for those who return to God, and his own prayer is an act of that return on behalf of the people.

words.note: Hesed, loving devotion or steadfast love, God's faithful covenant love. Nehemiah begins his prayer with the God “who keeps His covenant of loving devotion” (verse 5). His confidence rests not on Israel's record, which he confesses is poor, but on God's unfailing commitment.

Zakar, to remember. “Remember, I pray, the word” (verse 8) is not a suggestion that God has forgotten but a covenant plea, asking God to act on what he said. The verb becomes a signature of the book: Nehemiah repeatedly asks God to remember him (5:19; 13:14, 22, 31) and to remember his enemies.

Shuv, to turn or return, here in the sense of repentance. The promise Nehemiah quotes says that if the people return to God, he will return them to the land. The same verb carries both movements, and the book as a whole shows a people returning physically and still learning to return in heart.

Maal, to act unfaithfully, used in verse 8 in God's warning: “If you are unfaithful, I will scatter you among the nations.” It was the word for the sin Ezra confronted (Ezra 9-10), and Nehemiah acknowledges that the exile was its consequence.

christ: Nehemiah intercedes for his people, confesses their sins as his own, and then leaves a secure place in the royal court to go to a ruined city and rebuild it. These are patterns that the New Testament fills with greater meaning, not predictions in the text. Jesus wept over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41-44), interceded for his people (John 17), and left the glory he shared with the Father to take on the form of a servant (Philippians 2:6-8). The covenant promise Nehemiah claims, that God would gather his scattered people to the place he had chosen for his name, is taken up in the Gospels, where Jesus speaks of gathering Jerusalem's children as a hen gathers her brood (Matthew 23:37) and of his death gathering the scattered children of God into one (John 11:52).
questions: Nehemiah was comfortable and secure in Susa, yet the news from Jerusalem broke his heart. What news or need has moved you enough to change your plans?
Nehemiah's prayer reminds God of his own promises. How might praying Scripture back to God change the way you pray?
Nehemiah confessed that he and his father's house had sinned, though he was not personally responsible for the exile. Why might confessing shared sin matter before asking God for help?
